💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that while it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it.
  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.
  • It has been revealed that sangaré came to the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that while it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he noted.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

It has been revealed that sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Industry observers note that sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

In a recent development, athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move promptly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

It has been revealed that what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he remarked.

Industry observers note that but you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Recent findings suggest that often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré stated. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré stated it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré remarked; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation.
  • Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on Thursday night in a 62-33 vote, advancing legislation designed to streamline federal permitting for a broad range of projects, including housing.

Industry observers note that the permitting reform bill aims to cut regulatory delays and lower costs for major development projects in housing, energy infrastructure and transportation. It is likely one of the last bipartisan measures this Congress will vote on before the 120th Congress is sworn in shortly after the upcoming year.

Pro-housing groups strongly support the bill, but many environmental organizations oppose it, arguing that it would roll back necessary environmental protections and promote more fossil fuel consumption.

BAAJA now heads to the U.S. House of Representatives, which is widely expected to vote on the measure before the newly introduced Congress is sworn in on January 3. However, the clock is ticking, as the House is already on Thanksgiving recess. That leaves about a month for the House to either pass the Senate’s version or reconcile any differences between the two chambers.

If the bill doesn’t reach President Trump’s desk by January 3, the process would have to start over with the fresh Congress, which would likely change some of its provisions.

Many affordable and multifamily projects that rely on federal funding or assistance face regulatory hurdles that most privately financed housing developments avoid.

Recent findings suggest that these projects include those backed by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), and the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). Examples include housing built using public housing assistance, Community Development Block Grant (CDBG) funding, USDA housing loans, disaster relief funds and more.

Most notably, these federally backed housing projects must go through National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) reviews that don’t apply to most private- sector development projects.

According to recent reports, these reviews, critics argue, add an extra regulatory burden that can increase project timelines by a year or more. Critics further contend that NEPA and NHPA, while well-intentioned laws, are often used by NIMBY groups to delay or kill affordable housing development.

In response to these concerns, BAAJA would streamline NEPA reviews for housing development by:.

These changes would strengthen and expand provisions in the HOME Reform Act of 2025, a bill included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act that exempted small federal housing projects of 15 units or less from NEPA review.

BAAJA would similarly streamline NHPA reviews and narrow which projects trigger a review, allowing redevelopment projects involving older buildings to move forward more quickly.

Additionally, the bill would streamline Clean Water Act reviews, in effect speeding up federal wetlands permitting by shortening review timelines and limiting certain EPA interventions and legal challenges. It would also shorten Endangered Species Act consultation timelines and give states a larger role in federal reviews to reduce permitting delays for residential developments on land with protected species or habitats.

In a recent development, support for BAAJA spans much of the housing industry. Earlier this month, the National Association of Home Builders, YIMBY Action, Up for Growth Action and dozens of other housing organizations and homebuilder groups signed a letter urging the Senate to move the permitting reform package forward.

On Friday, National Association of REALTORS Executive Vice President and Chief Advocacy Officer Shannon McGahn stated in a statement she supports the legislation’s goal of streamlining “permitting processes and reducing unnecessary regulatory burdens that drive up development costs, delay construction and limit housing supply.”.

“These barriers affect everything from starter homes to multifamily rental housing, making it harder to meet the needs of buyers and renters alike,” McGahn stated.

NAHB further argued that BAAJA would reduce land development costs and permitting delays, while also improving multifamily builders’ access to federal housing finance programs. In a statement following the Senate’s vote, NAHB Chairman Bill Owens noted that the bill “will help builders deliver the affordable homes families need.”.

In a recent development, “By cutting the regulatory costs and delays that drive up the price of construction, BAAJA will expand housing supply, lower costs for buyers and renters and increase access to affordable rental housing. With so many families priced out of the market, the House must pass this bill without delay,” Owens said.

In a recent development, housing is only a fraction of what BAAJA targets. It mainly aims to streamline the development of a wide range of federally backed projects, including:.

As it does for housing, BAAJA would scale back NEPA and other environmental reviews for these federal projects, while also including other measures to shorten permitting and approval timelines.

In the Senate, 47 Republicans and 15 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted in favor of the bill.

Senators Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) and Josh Hawley (R-MO) were the only Republican Senators to vote against the legislation, largely because they feared it would undermine states’ rights.

In a recent development, meanwhile, 31 Democrats voted against it. The legislation has drawn significant opposition from environmental groups concerned that its permitting changes could weaken environmental protections and accelerate fossil fuel emissions.

Sierra Club Executive Director Loren Blackford, for example, argued that the bill “furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands and endangers wildlife.”.

Other critics of BAAJA worry that the bill’s permitting reforms could accelerate the development of more data centers, including on public lands.

Despite the ongoing opposition from environmental groups, BAAJA has bipartisan support in the House. For example, Rep. Scott Peters (D-CA), who backs the bill’s permitting provisions, countered these concerns by noting that it would also fast-track renewable energy development. He reiterated his support for the bill after it passed the Senate.

Industry observers note that “BAAJA lowers costs and lowers emissions. It’s that simple. It’s unimaginable that after this month’s election, when the entire country demanded lower costs, we would whiff on the opportunity right in front of us,” Peters remarked in a statement.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 8:52 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:12 am.

Industry observers note that update, Wednesday Nov. 18: ULA said Wednesday that preliminary findings indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from an inadequate fuel supply to its BE-4 engines, not the engines’ own performance. Read our latest story.

Early data suggests the first stage of United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket underperformed just after liftoff Sunday, leaving it unable to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit, ULA stated Tuesday.

In its first detailed account of the failure, ULA cited “low booster performance,” using its term for Vulcan’s core first stage. As a result, the stage separated when the rocket was too low and moving too slowly to reach orbit.

Industry observers note that that stage is powered by two BE-4 engines from Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin. However, ULA didn’t say what caused the shortfall or whether the engines played a role. ULA said it’s very early in the process and that it wants to avoid speculation until the investigation is complete.

The Centaur upper stage appears to have started normally, and its two L3Harris RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the shortfall, ULA stated. The six solid rocket boosters made by Northrop Grumman, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally.

The Federal Aviation Administration will oversee the ULA-led investigation and approve its final report, including any fixes.

What changed since Sunday: ULA’s account changes the picture from Sunday, when the failure appeared to come about 10 minutes into the flight, during the Centaur’s burn.

It has been revealed that ULA remarked Tuesday that it appears to have lost telemetry and the mission at about that point, but that the trouble began just after liftoff. Spaceflight Now reported Sunday that the first stage appeared to burn longer than planned before separating.

Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, asked on X why the Kent, Wash.-based tech giant hadn’t commented, replied Tuesday morning.

“It is ULA’s mission so they should provide the updates,” Limp wrote. “We are supporting them with data and analysis from the BE-4s. Team Blue continues to ready the pad and Fresh Glenn for our return to flight.”.

According to recent reports, impact on Amazon Leo: Sunday’s launch was the first of 38 Vulcan missions Amazon bought for its planned rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is slated to carry more than 1,500 of Amazon’s first-generation satellites, more than any other rocket in the program.

Amazon also has 24 introduces reserved on New Glenn, which uses seven BE-4s on its first stage. New Glenn has been grounded since an oxygen valve problem caused one to explode during a ground test in May. Blue Origin retrofitted the BE-4s on Sunday’s Vulcan with a fix for that problem, ULA CEO Mark Peller said before the flight.

Before Sunday, Amazon had launched 396 satellites for its Redmond-based Leo program on 14 successful missions since April 2025, most recently on an Atlas 5 in July. The Federal Communications Commission let Amazon keep deploying satellites after it fell short of a July 30 deadline to have 1,616 in service. Amazon still has until July 30, 2029, to deploy all 3,232 of its first-generation satellites.

Amazon has said it aims to start commercial internet service this year through Leo, formerly known as Project Kuiper. The next scheduled Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

#99126. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, want to price more precisely?
  • Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers remarked no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

Industry observers note that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

In a recent development, expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

Sources indicate that A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Industry observers note that imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

In a recent development, suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

It has been revealed that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

It has been revealed that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Sources indicate that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

According to recent reports, so, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

Sources indicate that twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that homeowners have spent the past several years holding onto low-rate first mortgages while looking for ways to access their accumulated home equity. As rates have stayed above pandemic-era lows, the lock-in effect has helped sustain demand for home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and second mortgages and is expected to continue into 2027.

According to a recent analysis from Benutech that examined county-level mortgage recording data, more than 6 million second mortgages, including home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and closed-end second liens, were recorded between Jan. 1, 2022, and Oct. 10, 2026.

Sources indicate that annual second-mortgage volume peaked in 2025 at 1.54 million loans, up 21.3% from 2024 and 32.4% from 2022. Through Oct. 10, 2026, 953,185 loans had been recorded, putting the market on pace for approximately 1.23 million loans for the year, the analysis found.

In October, a report from First American Data & Analytics found that U.S. homeowners held $13.2 trillion in accessible home equity in Q2 2026. Roughly 88% of that equity was tied to mortgages with rates below the market average.

In a recent development, the Federal Reserve Bank of Upcoming York’s Center for Microeconomic Data reported similar findings in its quarterly report on household debt and credit, released at the start of November. HELOC balances increased by $23 billion to $481 billion, marking the largest quarterly increase since 2005. HELOC limits also rose by $31 billion, extending an expansion that began in 2022.

As a result, the news cycle is abuzz with tales of borrowers turning to home equity products. But Anthony Stratis, vice president of lending partnerships at Figure, pointed out that demand has been building for several years, with homeowners using second liens to fund renovations and consolidate debt.

A significant share of Figure borrowers use home equity financing for those purposes, he said.

Stratis said the demand could outlast the current interest-rate environment as lenders improve their products and borrowers become more accustomed to using home equity to access cash.

Industry observers note that “Home equity has really evolved to the point where it’s a pretty quick way to access cash when you need it for a project or whatever it might be,” Stratis said. “I think that part is going to stay in place, and home equity is likely to have a place in the mortgage ecosystem for a while, independent of rates.”.

Matt Kroon, a home loan specialist at Churchill Mortgage, pointed out the “emotional connection” that borrowers have with their low, COVID-era mortgage rates. But persistently high rates and an aging home stock have led borrowers to inquire about other solutions.

“Since affordability is a major concern right now, people are accessing their equity to make those improvements, or to pay off any higher-interest debt,” Kroon remarked. “Renovations and debt consolidation HELOCs are the main uses right now. However, some other uses include major expenses like a newly introduced roof, siding, furnace, etc.”.

Tom Hutchens, president of Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions, agreed with Stratis that his firm has seen steady HELOC demand over the past several years. Angel Oak, a non-QM lender, sees most of its demand among self-employed borrowers and those who use bank statement documentation to qualify for both first mortgages and HELOCs.

Hutchens stated borrowers are also using home equity to pay down high-interest credit card balances. Angel Oak’s average combined loan-to-value ratio on HELOCs is in the 60% range, he said.

“Private capital is getting into the HELOC business. You’re going to start to see more and more HELOC securitizations,” he added.

Kevin Leibowitz, founder of Grayton Mortgage, said that while HELOC inquiries have increased, not all conversations result in second mortgages.

Recent findings suggest that “[There is] lots of interest in HELOCs, a lot of production in HELOCs,” Leibowitz said. “But a lot of my conversations start with HELOCs, and we kind of pivot into other types of lending because the other types of lending might make sense.”.

The decision often comes down to comparing the cost of a borrower’s existing debt with the rate available on a new loan, he noted. While borrowers may be reluctant to refinance a low-rate first mortgage, high-interest credit card balances and other obligations can make a new first mortgage more advantageous.

Benjamin Cohen, managing director and SVP of mortgage lending at Rate, said borrowers who might have done a cash-out refinance in the past are now looking at a HELOC or a fixed-rate second mortgage like our HELoan.

Industry observers note that “The math is pretty straightforward. If you owe $500,000 at 3% and need another $75,000, a cash-out refinance puts the entire $575,000 at today’s rate,” Cohen mentioned. “With a second mortgage, you keep the $500,000 at 3% and pay the latest rate only on the $75,000. Even if the second mortgage carries a higher rate than the cash-out refinance, your blended rate across both loans can still be meaningfully lower. That can be a good compromise if the payments, fees and repayment terms make sense for you.”.

Leibowitz cited one borrower who had accumulated significant credit card debt after being laid off. By replacing the borrower’s first and second mortgages along with the credit card debt, he mentioned, he improved the borrower’s monthly cash flow by about $3,500.

Industry observers note that for borrowers with relatively low first-mortgage rates, keeping that loan and adding a HELOC may still be the better option. But HELOCs typically carry variable rates tied to the Wall Street Journal prime rate, exposing borrowers to higher payments if rates rise, Leibowitz noted.

Adam Hopson, chief operating officer of Flyhomes, said home equity can also help homeowners purchase another property before selling their current one. However, the additional borrowing can affect their ability to qualify for a latest mortgage.

“A HELOC can unlock a down payment without unlocking a move,” Hopson said. “Having access to equity and qualifying for the next mortgage are two different things, though.”.

According to recent reports, the largest Shiba Inu traders and investors moved more than 6 billion SHIB to exchange addresses out of the blue, potentially chasing liquidity instead of holding. For now, SHIB hasn't reacted to the transfer, as moving SHIB to exchanges doesn't guarantee immediate selling.

According to recent reports, it could be a sign, though: according to historical data, whale activity quite often corresponds to market improvements for SHIB. Those whales might have certain data that we don't.

Sources indicate that whenever the price moves up, whales who accumulated previously liquidate their holdings and successfully move on. However, it's not a paramount rule that can't be broken. We might always see a flip in that tendency.

Retail investors aren't moving on par with those 6 billion, data suggests, as inflow and outflow data show neutrality rather than leaning in one direction or the other.

The timing of the transfer is somewhat interesting: the market isn't recovering, SHIB is losing the ground it has gained in the last few days, and, unfortunately, the SHIB sent to exchanges might contribute to a further price drop.

SHIB is oversold, clearly, but the presence of supply just sitting elsewhere essentially enables the possibility of a quick drop way sooner than we might think.

The key here is the lack of proper psychological and technical levels that might help the price recover or at least form a range.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:38 pm.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella opened his Ignite keynote Tuesday in San Francisco by addressing the elephant in the room: the global Outlook outage that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries last week.

Before getting to Copilot, agents or any of the event’s news, Nadella said the outage was a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure has become as “the dial tone for the world.”.

“We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously,” he stated. “And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.”.

The line drew applause from the crowd, interrupting Nadella as he moved to thank the IT pros in the audience who kept their own organizations running through the outage.

Industry observers note that it was a brief acknowledgment, and he didn’t go into what went wrong. Microsoft’s preliminary report blamed a bug in a fix it began rolling out in July, which its own automatic rerouting spread until most of the servers in a key Microsoft 365 gateway stopped responding. A final report is due Nov. 20.

Industry observers note that from there, Nadella moved on to the main show. Watch the keynote below, and see updates here.

The Single Asset Vault amendment on the XRP Ledger is getting closer to activation on the mainnet as validator support builds for the network’s preparation to enable better DeFi functionality.

In a recent development, according to data from XRPScan, the SingleAssetVault amendment, or XLS-65, has received yes votes from 25 of 35 trusted validators, currently standing at 71.43% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of 35 votes (29) to start its 14-day countdown to activation. That means it needs four more votes to get there and could reach the magic number before the end of 2026.

The XRP Ledger’s amendment process requires a proposed amendment to be approved by more than 80% of trusted validators for 14 days before it is implemented. Validator support may shift during this time, and if the required 80% threshold is lost, activation may be delayed.

The Single Asset Vault amendment creates a structure for aggregating assets from multiple depositors and is intended to be used with the on-chain Lending Protocol. The amendment introduces a Vault object that defines the state of a tokenized vault, and the Vault entry is one of the ledger entry types it provides.

It has been revealed that the Vault object holds important information such as available assets, shares, total value, and other relevant information. Users can create a Vault object with the VaultCreate transaction; the Vault object is tracked in an Owner Directory owned by the Vault Owner account.

According to recent reports, the XRP Ledger lending amendment has gained additional yes votes. According to XRPScan, the LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment, also known as XLS-66, has received 24 yes votes out of 35 trusted validators, meaning it has 68.57% consensus as of November 18, 2026. It needs more than 80% of the 35 votes (29) to trigger a 14-day activation countdown.

This implies that there are five votes left for it to reach this threshold, with the possibility of it securing the required number of votes before the end of 2026 as well.

According to XRP enthusiasts, LendingProtocolV1_1 represents the biggest amendment for unlocking capital and liquidity on the XRP Ledger and is anticipated by institutional and retail people.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bronx real estate broker Marcia Campbell was arrested and indicted for allegedly failing to disclose felony convictions and pending criminal charges when she applied to renew her Latest York real estate broker license, New York Attorney General Letitia James declared Thursday.

Sources indicate that campbell, 64, who operates Extreme Realty Associates Inc. in the Bronx, is accused of falsely stating on a June 2026 renewal application that she had not been convicted of a crime and had no criminal charges pending since her previous renewal, according to the announcement from the Office of the Attorney General (OAG).

Industry observers note that state regulators say that during that June 14, 2024, to June 13, 2026, period, Campbell had in fact pleaded guilty to two felonies in Westchester County and was facing 18 pending charges in Bronx County tied to alleged deed theft and real estate investment scams. Once the Fresh York Department of State (DOS) discovered the alleged false statements, her broker license was administratively suspended.

The case underscores how aggressively Latest York regulators and prosecutors are now scrutinizing license applications and renewals for real estate professionals, particularly in deed theft and fraud matters. For brokers and agents, the case is a reminder that criminal history disclosures on licensing forms are not procedural formalities, but sworn statements that can carry separate felony exposure if falsified.

The latest indictment builds on a series of criminal matters involving Campbell in multiple counties.

In October 2024, Attorney General James and Bronx District Attorney Darcel Clark announced two separate indictments against Campbell. In the first, she and her co-conspirators — including her husband — were charged in an alleged deed theft scheme involving the childhood home of a Bronx woman. Prosecutors say the group gained the homeowner’s trust, then used fraudulent contracts bearing the homeowner’s forged signature to transfer the property to a shell company they controlled and to obtain a $493,500 mortgage on the home. Campbell is scheduled to go to trial in that case on Feb. 22, 2027.

Sources indicate that the second Bronx indictment accused Campbell of running a series of real estate investment scams. According to prosecutors, she induced clients to send her funds for purported real estate transactions, then kept the money and refused to return most of it. Those alleged scams took more than $250,000 from vulnerable New Yorkers, including first-time homebuyers, immigrants and a personal friend, the OAG mentioned. A trial date in those cases has not yet been set.

Sources indicate that separate Westchester County prosecutions led to criminal convictions. On Dec. 18, 2025, Campbell pleaded guilty in two cases to Falsifying Business Records in the First Degree and Repeated Failure to File Corporate Taxes, both class E felonies. Authorities stated those cases involved an alleged deed theft scheme that targeted three Westchester homes and involved roughly $2 million in fraudulently obtained loans. Campbell was sentenced to time served in those matters.

Sources indicate that despite those developments, prosecutors say Campbell submitted a broker license renewal application to DOS in June 2026 covering the period from June 15, 2026, through June 13, 2028. On that application, she allegedly answered “no” to questions asking whether she had been convicted of a crime or had criminal charges pending during the prior licensing period.

Attorney General James alleges Campbell knowingly omitted her December 2025 felony convictions in Westchester County and the 18 Bronx County charges that were already pending at the time she filed the renewal. When DOS identified the discrepancies and referred the matter to law enforcement, the agency suspended Campbell’s license.

For brokerages, the case highlights the operational risk of failing to monitor the criminal and regulatory status of principal brokers and associated licensees. A suspended or revoked license can jeopardize transactions, commissions and firm reputation, especially in markets where deed theft has drawn heightened scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators.

Fresh York officials at the state and local level have invested significant resources into deed theft enforcement in recent years, particularly in New York City and surrounding counties where equity-rich but cash-poor homeowners are frequent targets. These schemes often rely on trusted intermediaries, including licensed real estate professionals, to gain access to property records and homeowners.

“New Yorkers depend on real estate brokers to help them make some of the most vital purchases of their lives,” Attorney General James remarked in the announcement, adding that Campbell allegedly abused her role “to steal New Yorkers’ homes and savings, then tried to hide her crimes to maintain her license.”.

Recent findings suggest that for compliance officers at brokerages and franchisors, the case signals that state regulators are willing to cross-check licensing records with court and tax data and to bring independent criminal charges based solely on false or incomplete filings. Firms may want to revisit internal policies requiring prompt disclosure of arrests and convictions by licensed personnel and procedures for verifying those disclosures.

  • Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:50 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026.

In a recent development, crowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.

Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through.

Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%.

Recent findings suggest that software buyouts tend to value the acquired firm at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.

CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.

Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a manufacturer’s employees access its business applications.

Enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.

Zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.

The company’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical issues that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.

Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.

The potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The manufacturer’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end people’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity problems.

Tech Report: Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

Recent findings suggest that the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont stated in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

Recent findings suggest that seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an key step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel stated. “I think it’s key to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

Industry observers note that “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker stated. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.
  • Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon.
  • Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club confirmed Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:02 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:02 am.

Chee Chew helped build the Windows 95 Start menu, started Google Hangouts and ran consumer engagement at Amazon. Now the Seattle tech veteran is taking on a upcoming job with the Sounders and Reign FC, where he’ll lead how the soccer clubs use technology, data and AI.

Chew, a minority owner of Sounders FC since 2019, is joining the organization’s executive team as chief technology and transformation officer, reporting to majority owner Adrian Hanauer, the club confirmed Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that “His knowledge of and passion for the Sounders and Reign allow him to hit the ground running,” Hanauer stated in a statement. “His experience leading teams through major shifts in technology gives us a unique opportunity to strengthen both the soccer and business sides of our organization.”.

Chew most recently was chief product and technology officer at Zapier, where he helped steer the workflow automation manufacturer toward AI. Before that he was chief product officer at mParticle and at Twilio, where he oversaw the communications company’s $3.2 billion acquisition of Segment.

He spent four years at Amazon, nearly eight years as a vice president of engineering at Google, where he also led the company’s Seattle and Kirkland offices, and 14 years at Microsoft working on Internet Explorer, Windows Mobile and Xbox Live.

It has been revealed that chew said his direct team will stay small, but its work will reach every corner of the business, including HR, ticket sales, customer service, match-day planning, corporate partnerships, legal, and player recruiting and scouting. He also wants every department to have its own “builders,” staffers who can create AI tools and automations for their own teams.

In a recent development, “In order to do a change like this, it’s more than technology,” Chew told GeekWire. “Technology is in many ways the easiest part. Driving change, getting deep, building side by side with folks, I think is what it takes.”.

Industry observers note that chew didn’t grow up playing soccer. “My family was a very traditional Chinese family of study and play piano,” he remarked. “It was a stereotype, but it was true for my family.” He caught the bug in college, where he played a ton of intramurals, and later from his wife, Christine, who played through college, and their two kids.

The couple joined the Sounders ownership group in 2019 as one of 11 Seattle-rooted families, many with deep ties to the region’s tech industry. Former Microsoft executive Terry Myerson pulled the group together, and it included Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, CFO Amy Hood, and others.

A group of owners has met every other Friday since 2019, and “leveraging technology has always been part of the strategy” for the club, Chew stated.

Industry observers note that the job grew out of a demo Chew built for Hanauer about two and a half years ago: an AI agent that could handle complicated fan requests, such as a season ticket holder with four seats who wants to buy a block of eight. The club later brought in consultants to train staff on AI, but the effort never quite gained momentum, he said.

Recent findings suggest that talks about a bigger role started early this year and came together by midyear. “Adrian and I talked about it, and we agreed for me to come on board and take an operational role and hack on some code,” Chew said.

According to recent reports, chew describes Hanauer as a visionary on “the art of the possible” who comes in daily asking, “Could you do this?” Recently, as Chew was boarding a flight home to Seattle, Hanauer called from a meeting where staff doubted they could scale up one effort tenfold without hiring more people. Could AI help?

On the flight, while using the plane’s Wi-Fi, he built a prototype with Anthropic’s Claude. “By the time I landed, I sent it to them and mentioned, ‘OK, give this a try,’” he said. The club used it in an experiment to scale up performance marketing before a match.

It’s the kind of hands-on building Chew says he’s been doing a lot of lately.

“I think I’ve created more code in the past six months than I did in the past 20 years,” he said. “It’s pretty amazing. I’m having a ton of fun.”.

Chew is also working with players.

Sources indicate that he recently ran an AI analysis of one player’s game, based on stats such as touches, expected goals and distance run. It pointed out strengths and areas to improve. The player was “very hungry for it,” Chew mentioned, and asked if they could do it every game.

The club’s performance analytics group, led by data analyst Tyler Cox, was already ahead of much of the organization, and Chew noted he’s helping speed up that work with AI.

The bigger challenge is getting people to change how they work, Chew said. At Zapier, he saw many companies struggle to get results from AI, with some spending “massive token budgets” without a substantial win. He said the answer is blending AI with traditional automation and fitting it into how people already work.

“It has to be approachable for folks,” he said. “You can’t go in and just throw everything up and start from scratch.”.

Industry observers note that the Sounders host Real Salt Lake in the wild-card round of the MLS Cup Playoffs on Thursday at Lumen Field. Asked whether AI could help figure out a win, Chew passed.

“I don’t want to get involved and interfere with our coaching staff,” he stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although XRP has achieved a sharp price rally after the severe price correction seen in the past months, its recent recovery has yet to influence the performance of its ETF market.
  • Latest data from SoSoValue indicates that momentum across the XRP ETF market has remained slow as the funds have continued to post massive withdrawals during each trading session in recent days.
  • Data highlights that the XRP ETFs managed by Canary Capital and Grayscale recorded combined withdrawals of $6.14 million during their latest trading session on November 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although XRP has achieved a sharp price rally after the severe price correction seen in the past months, its recent recovery has yet to influence the performance of its ETF market.

Latest data from SoSoValue indicates that momentum across the XRP ETF market has remained slow as the funds have continued to post massive withdrawals during each trading session in recent days.

Data highlights that the XRP ETFs managed by Canary Capital and Grayscale recorded combined withdrawals of $6.14 million during their latest trading session on November 17.

This also represents the total daily net outflows recorded on that day as only the two funds were active while the rest of the XRP ETF products remained muted with zero participation from investors.

While this means that investors have continued to withdraw their funds despite XRP attempting to reclaim the $1 price level, Canary Capital's XRP ETF saw the highest withdrawal of the day.

Notably, the fund recorded over 5 million XRP, worth about $5.01 million, in daily outflows, while Grayscale's XRP ETF followed with just $1.12 million in outflows.

Although Bitwise did not record any inflow or outflow on this day, the firm still stands as XRP’s biggest ETF manager as it controls over $392.64 million in net assets as of this date.

Despite its dominance in the XRP ETF market, Bitwise has remained muted all week, showing zero daily participation since November 9, when it posted its highest-ever daily outflow of $9.40 million.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meredith Wimbrow is leaving her role as director of stakeholder relations at the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) after about 20 months to become a vice president at Federal Hall Policy Advisors, she told HousingWire.

Wimbrow, a former FHFA Director Bill Pulte aide, is joining the private sector. POLITICO first reported on her transition. FHFA did not immediately respond to a request for comments.

“I had a great experience at FHFA. It gave me firsthand understanding of the housing finance system and the policy making process, and the importance of the relationship between the government and the agency,” Wimbrow remarked. “My role there was stakeholder relations. So I had a great opportunity to engage with the industry and work with folks in the housing space.”.

During her tenure, Wimbrow said key discussions with industry participants focused on affordability, credit score modernization, oversight of the government-sponsored enterprises (GSEs) and the future of the housing finance system, as well as insurance modernization.

“The industry was very positive with the engagement, and they appreciated the focus of making housing affordable,” she noted.

Wimbrow framed the career move as a natural shift from public service to advisory work.

“I wanted to take what I learned on the agency side, particularly in stakeholder relations and industry engagement, and apply that experience in the private sector,” Wimbrow mentioned. “It’s a natural step for me to decide on Fed Hall; they lobbied me, and they’re the best in the business.”.

Before joining FHFA, Wimbrow spent three years at the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), most recently as director of Build-PAC, NAHB’s bipartisan political arm focused on federal campaigns.

Seattle police unleash dog-like robot whose best trick is bomb dispoal

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am.
  • Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech.
  • According to recent reports, the department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:43 amNovember 17, 2026 at 11:43 am.

Seattle police already have a dog that sniffs out tech. Now they’ve got a piece of tech that looks like a dog.

According to recent reports, the department’s Arson/Bomb Squad is now using a Spot robot from Boston Dynamics, bought with a Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that the Seattle City Council approved in April after a review of privacy and security risks. Bomb technicians can steer the robot from nearly a mile away to inspect suspicious devices, open doors and move possible explosives into safe containers, SPD mentioned in a blog post last week.

It’s a massive upgrade for the squad, which has handled more than 600 calls so far this year. SPD’s main bomb robot is nearly 20 years old, weighs more than 100 pounds and rolls on tracks, and it can only be hauled around in the squad’s mobile workshop. Spot weighs under 100 pounds, climbs stairs and rides in a pickup truck that bomb techs drive daily.

SPD also spelled out what Spot won’t do.

The robot will only be used for explosive threats in the city and at the port, and it won’t carry a weapon. SPD noted a weapon would go against Boston Dynamics’ rules for its robots. Spot’s 360-degree camera sends an encrypted live feed to the operator but doesn’t record or use facial recognition.

The only thing the robot does on its own is open a door, after an operator lines it up. As one bomb technician put it in SPD’s post, Spot will “be as dumb in 10 years as it is today.”.

It’s not the first time SPD has turned to a four-legged partner for tech-related work.

Nala, an electronic storage detection K9 — profiled by GeekWire in 2024 — is trained to smell a chemical compound used in making electronics. The Labrador retriever helps SPD’s Internet Crimes Against Children task force find hidden phones, hard drives and micro SD cards during warrant searches. Her handler, Det. Daljit Gill, told GeekWire at the time that Nala turns up a device human searchers missed about 30% of the time.

Spot appears decidedly less cuddly.

Industry observers note that boston Dynamics, maker of backflipping Atlas humanoids and other viral-video robots, first unveiled the robodog in 2015. A smaller, all-electric version followed a year later.

Sources indicate that the machines have long stirred dystopian unease. A 2017 “Black Mirror” episode featured killer robot dogs inspired by the tech giant’s designs. Still, Spot has turned up in friendlier settings: then-Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos walked one at the company’s MARS conference in 2018 — a scene described by GeekWire’s Alan Boyle as featuring the “anxiety-inducing” robot.

Recent findings suggest that police departments have embraced the robots, too. More than 60 bomb squads and SWAT teams in the U.S. and Canada use Spot, Bloomberg reported last year, including a regional bomb unit in Portland. Upcoming York police returned one in 2021 after public backlash, then brought the robots back two years later.

Recent findings suggest that back in Seattle, SPD’s bomb technicians see more potential uses down the road, according to the department’s post, including communicating and observing from a distance as part of de-escalation. For now, Spot’s job is limited to explosives.

And the robot won’t be getting a latest name, SPD stated, “because it is not a toy, or a dog, even though it kind of looks like both.”.

‘More Secret’ Version of Bitcoin: Zcash (ZEC) Eyes Another Wall Street ETF

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • Asset manager Bitwise has filed an S-1 with the U.S.
  • Industry observers note that zcash is often called a "more secret" version of Bitcoin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Asset manager Bitwise has filed an S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a spot Zcash (ZEC) exchange-traded fund. The document appeared in the SEC's database on Nov. 17, 2026. On Wednesday, ZEC rose to $975 before it pulled back to around $927.

Industry observers note that zcash is often called a "more secret" version of Bitcoin. According to the S-1, the Zcash network supports two types of transactions, and the "shielded" ones use a form of zero-knowledge cryptography known as zk-SNARKs. Holders of shielded Zcash "may selectively disclose transaction information to third parties," the filing says.

Recent findings suggest that bitwise's fund will not use this feature. "The Trust does not engage in shielded transactions in connection with its activities," according to the document.

In a recent development, the shares are expected to list on the Dallas-based Texas Stock Exchange (TXSE) under the ticker ZEC. According to the S-1, Coinbase Custody Trust Company will act as the Zcash custodian, and BNY Mellon will serve as the cash custodian. Bitwise also wrote that "the Trust will not stake or otherwise seek to derive additional Zcash from its holdings." The sponsor fee in the filing is listed as "0.___% per annum.".

In the risk section of the S-1, Bitwise wrote that "a number of digital asset trading platforms have delisted Zcash, restricted trading in Zcash or declined to support Zcash." According to the filing, many of these platforms cited regulatory or compliance concerns.

The platforms that still support Zcash "do so only with respect to transparent addresses and do not permit deposits or withdrawals to or from shielded addresses," the document states. Bitwise also pointed to new EU rules that take effect on July 10, 2027. According to the S-1, the rules will "prohibit credit institutions, financial institutions and crypto-asset service providers in the European Union" from keeping accounts in such assets.

Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan named Zcash one of his top three assets for the decade in September, alongside Bitcoin and tokenization projects. Three days before the S-1 filing, he called ZEC a "golden mean" between open Bitcoin and anonymous Monero in an interview.

Industry observers note that grayscale's Zcash fund (ZCSH) has traded on NYSE Arca since August 2026, and the Winklevoss brothers filed for their own Zcash ETF on Nasdaq in October. ZCSH held $496.79 million as of the Nov. 17 close, according to SoSoValue. The fund has attracted $168.76 million in net inflows since its launch, and it recorded no inflows on Nov. 17, when Bitwise filed its S-1.

Howard Hanna sued over $395 real estate transaction fee

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.
  • Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.
  • Bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is joining the growing roster of real estate firms facing a lawsuit over a “transaction fee” a consumer was allegedly forced to pay in conjunction with their real estate transaction.

Earlier this month, first-time homebuyer Dena Bergamasco filed a suit against Howard Hanna over a $395 “Realtor Transaction Fee” she claims she was charged on top of the buyer broker commission she paid related to her October 2021 home purchase.

Bergamasco is being represented by Kopelowitz Ostrow P.A. one of the firms representing plaintiff Gregory Deivert in his transaction fee lawsuit filed against a Keller Williams franchise last month.

Attorneys for Bergamasco claim in the filing that as her buyer broker Howard Hanna breached its fiduciary duty and violated the state’s Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law in charging her this fee, which the suit describes as a “cash grab.”.

Bargamasco claims that the $395 fee was charged “for nothing” with “no service behind it, no cost behind it, and no name that accurately describes it.”.

“It is money taken from a client by the broker who was supposed to be looking out for her,” the complaint states.

It has been revealed that according to the complaint, the fee was “wedged”  between third-party charges for a pest inspection fee and an owner’s title insurance premium in the closing disclosure. Additionally, the complaint alleges that the brokerage coaches agents to tell clients that the fee is mandatory and serves a “processing” or “administrative” purpose.

According to recent reports, in the filing, Bergamasco’s attorneys state that she paid $217,000 for her home, with $213,069 of this coming from a federally insured mortgage and $10,850 coming from a second loan from the Pennsylvania Housing Finance Agency. In addition to this, the sellers awarded her a $7,300 credit to use toward closing costs. In total, the filing states that Bergamasco brought $788.95 in cash to her closing, not even double the cost of the alleged fee. According to the filing, with the home purchase transaction occurring prior to the Sitzer/Burnett commission lawsuit settlement, the plaintiff’s buyer broker commission was paid by the home seller and that Bergamasco paid for the paperwork completed by the settlement agent and title insurance provider at the closing.

Sources indicate that the suit is seeking class action status and the plaintiff has demanded a jury trial. Bergamasco remarked she is seeking damages and a permanent injunction preventing Howard Hanna from charging this fee in the future.

Howard Hanna did not immediately return HousingWire’s request for comment regarding the lawsuit.

The complaint claims that the practice of charging consumers a “transaction fee” is not unique to Howard Hanna. This is evidenced in the other lawsuits that have popped up this year, including the lawsuit against Keller Williams Elite over an alleged $650 “broker fee” and a since voluntarily dismissed lawsuit filed against Compass over an alleged $475 transaction fee.

Some reports, such as one from the Consumer Policy Center, claim that consumers pay up to $2 billion in brokerage transaction fees each year.

#99106. Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm.
  • Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers.
  • “Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” noted Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the organization’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm.

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” noted Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the organization’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Recent findings suggest that jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he mentioned.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou stated.

Sources indicate that microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” people of each manufacturer’s agent tools, it revealed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

It has been revealed that the numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced upcoming Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

It has been revealed that the companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly people as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report stated.

Newly introduced MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft indicates it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Industry observers note that microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Organization consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Industry observers note that keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

Recent findings suggest that the cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Industry observers note that microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A newly introduced Agent 365 Business Analytics feature reveals business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

#99105. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1530 w)
