Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I run a global business called Brand of a Leader, which supports founders and executives in more than 12 countries by helping them build their visibility. When I first introduced my business six years ago, all I had was a LinkedIn profile — no website and, naturally, no digital footprint of any kind yet.

In a recent development, and so our first few clients came through my network. By being active on LinkedIn and consistently sharing my perspective, I would stay top of mind with people who already knew me. When they needed support, or when someone in their own network did, I was the one who came to mind and was hired or recommended.

Today, I continue to use LinkedIn actively to generate clients, develop relationships and stay connected with my network. I’ve been on the platform for over 20 years, and throughout the years, I’ve heard people constantly complain about one thing: the algorithm. I always chuckle because the discourse is consistently the same, yet it’s presented as something fresh. Through all of my work and my extensive work supporting founders across the globe with their LinkedIn, I’ve seen how much people overindex on what to post, when to post and how to post, while overlooking something else that is likely even more important!

Here are the three mistakes I see founders make all the time. And I promise that if you fix those, you will see better results from this platform.

Obsession over what, when and how to post is real. Short posts or long posts? Daily or weekly? With a photo? Video? No media? What should I even write about? Those are undoubtedly notable questions, yet there’s another one: What happens when someone reads your post, does become interested in learning more about you and then clicks on your profile?

My experience demonstrates me that most founders don’t pay much attention to what’s actually on their profile. I know this because I constantly audit LinkedIn pages as part of the service that we provide at Brand of a Leader.

Too often, when I visit a LinkedIn profile, I find a bland banner or none whatsoever, and a short “About” section written in the third person. Whatever interest the person’s post may have piqued is quickly lost when visiting their uninspiring profile.

Personally, I treat my profile as a landing page. And we do the same for our clients. For entrepreneurs, myself included, a well-designed LinkedIn page can be a practical alternative to a personal website when used thoughtfully.

Visit your profile, looking at it through the eyes of a potential client, and see what impression it would leave on them after spending a minute or two scrolling through it.

It has been revealed that one of the things we consistently convince our clients not to do is include calls to action in their posts. Salesy or overly promotional messages on founders’ profiles don’t make a great impression.

Recent findings suggest that as a reader, I find that repeated prompts to book a call can make otherwise thoughtful writing feel overly promotional. I prefer to keep my content, and my clients’ content, conversational, expertise-building or humanizing. Yet, I do understand the importance of giving interested readers a clearly visible way to take the next step.

Instead of salesy calls to action in posts, I leverage the custom call-to-action button included with LinkedIn Premium Business. You can have it say anything that’s most relevant to you and your goals (for example, “Visit my website” or “Book a call”). This link will appear in your profile, just under your name and above the post that you write. That feels more elegant to me.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest mistakes I see founders make is treating LinkedIn as a broadcasting platform and not a social media platform. This is not only the quickest way to reduce the overall engagement of your content on LinkedIn, but it’s also not great for your positioning overall. When you only post and never engage, it positions you as a taker, not a giver, and also discourages people from further engaging with you.

Recent findings suggest that at a minimum, you need to reply to people who took the time to comment on your posts. No, not only a “like” — an actual thoughtful reply. They have taken time to respond to something you shared. Read their contribution and respond to the substance of it.

And then ideally, extend that attention to other people’s content. Comment to share a relevant experience or ask a thoughtful question. If someone describes a challenge you have faced, explain what you learned. But don’t use AI. Generic, bland comments negatively impact your brand equity. Take 30 minutes to leave some authentic comments a couple of times weekly, and that consistency will compound over time.

Industry observers note that before publishing your next post, think about what interested readers will see on your profile if they click on it. Give them enough context to understand your expertise, an easy way to contact you and your attention when they engage in conversation with you.

Recent findings suggest that before you hit publish again, take a look at LinkedIn’s upcoming Small Business Playbook for practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make sure your profile is ready when interested readers click through.

To protect its users and to ensure a high-quality trading market, Binance conducts regular reviews of all listed spot trading pairs; it may delist certain spot trading pairs for various reasons, including low liquidity and trading volume.

Binance will delist GAS/TRY, HBAR/BNB, HIVE/TRY, KSM/TRY and ZAMA/TRY pairs on November 20, 2026 at 03:00 UTC, according to an official announcement published on November 18.

Industry observers note that binance will terminate Spot Trading Bots services for the spot trading pairs simultaneously where applicable. Users are strongly advised to update and/or cancel their Spot Trading Bots prior to the cessation of services for Spot Trading Bots to avoid any potential losses.

Industry observers note that in related news, Binance Margin will initiate a routine cleanup of Cross Margin accounts with collateral valued at less than 1 USD (or equivalent in other assets), effective from November 30, 2026 at 00:00 (UTC). The cleanup will be executed on a daily basis as an ongoing operational process.

In a recent development, affected accounts include Cross Margin Accounts with a collateral value of less than 1 USD equivalent across all assets and no outstanding liabilities, as well as Margin Accounts with no capital activity in the past 6 months. Capital activity refers to any action that generates a capital flow.

For each eligible Small-Asset Account, the system will automatically transfer the collateral in users’ Margin Accounts to their Spot Accounts while the Margin Account functions remain normal, allowing users to transfer, borrow, or trade at any time after the cleanup.

Accounts with collateral equal to or exceeding 1 USD equivalent are not affected by this cleanup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sister will provide. True, French Gates mentioned, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

It has been revealed that paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sources indicate that sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers noted they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

In a recent development, she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In a recent development, in its own analysis, The Newly introduced York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates remarked she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Recent findings suggest that as the fourth quarter rolls around, entrepreneurs everywhere hope to close out a productive year. This season sparks a flurry of activity for businesses, especially those eager to capitalize on fall and holiday shoppers. No matter your industry, the holiday season is the ideal moment to highlight the power of genuine human connection.

According to recent reports, AI can accomplish a lot, but it still falls short when it comes to the magic of personal touch. It’s easy to see how positive human interaction can boost your business during the holidays, but these same tactics belong in your everyday playbook. Let’s explore a few simple ways the human touch can spark joy that goes far beyond your bottom line.

According to recent reports, I have to confess, there are moments when I catch myself sounding like someone from an older generation. Every day, I remind my staff to return client calls promptly and reply to emails without delay. Though I’m only in my late 40s, I notice a shift in my younger colleagues. Like a fading sense of urgency and a dwindling desire for personal interaction.

Perhaps it’s a wish to sidestep conflict or uncomfortable conversations. I understand that urge. Still, I’ve learned that the fastest way to resolve a tough client situation is through genuine human touch. I’m not referring to physical touch, but honest, direct communication delivered with empathy and understanding. On the other hand, leading with human touch from the start can forge deeper bonds and lasting appreciation with customers.

You’ve probably heard the saying, “size matters.” While that might hold true in some cases, my own transcription company is small compared to many others. Yet, the personal touch we practice and that I encourage my team to deliver works just as well for medium and large businesses alike.

Recent findings suggest that most of our first interactions with clients begin on our website, where a potential customer fills out our contact form. That’s our first chance to connect personally, to reach out and add a human touch. Here’s an example of how a team member might respond to a website inquiry.

Industry observers note that “Thanks for reaching out, Jane. We’d love to assist you with your court hearing transcripts. When do you need them completed and sent back?”.

Let’s unpack our initial email. First, we always address the person by name. If they include a title, we use it, whether it’s Dr. Smith or Detective Jones. Second, we acknowledge their inquiry as swiftly as possible, ideally within 15 minutes. Finally, we ask for permission to connect more personally. A phone conversation with a potential customer lets us highlight our services and, even more importantly, our commitment to detail.

Most people appreciate the chance to talk by phone. For those who prefer email, there are still plenty of ways to add a personal touch throughout the exchange. Whether we’re on the phone or typing an email, we make it a point to ask open-ended questions that encourage the other person to share more. This is a classic strategy sales trainers recommend everywhere.

The holiday season offers your team even more chances to make a lasting impression through personal interaction. We keep it simple with a cheerful “Happy Holidays,” but if a client mentions a specific celebration, i.e., Thanksgiving, Christmas, Hanukkah or Kwanzaa, then we ask how they are enjoying their favorite season.

Finally, our team always aims to have the last word. When a customer pays an invoice, we don’t just send an automated “Thank you for your payment.” Instead, we follow up with a personal email to our main contact, giving us one more opportunity to add a genuine human touch.

What exactly will your business or company gain through human touch? Trust. Customers, more specifically, individuals, want to know they can trust you to deliver a service or product.

It’s true that most companies can build some trust without much human interaction. If you add a personal touch, it speeds up the process and makes it feel more genuine. Too often, human interaction only happens when something goes wrong. While it’s smart to use a personal approach to solve problems, starting every client relationship with a human touch lays a strong foundation for when challenges pop up later.

Sources indicate that people with a personal relationship with an employee or firm respond to challenges very differently than those without one. That’s simply human nature.

Industry observers note that personally, I get frustrated when I can’t reach a real person with a question or concern. Endless phone trees and chatbots that never connect you to a human leave me feeling anything but trust. Here are a few ways to boost human interaction:.

Sources indicate that if Emily Post, the famed etiquette expert of the early 20th century, were still with us, I’m sure she’d have plenty to say about the power of handwritten notes. Even though I haven’t found a definitive study on their impact, my own experience tells me that few things leave a stronger impression than a personally written letter or note.

I think the magic of a handwritten note starts with the effort it takes. Printing a form letter or invoice is easy, but writing a note by hand and addressing the envelope takes real time and care. Even jotting a quick sentence or two at the bottom of a printed letter can make a lasting impression.

Recent findings suggest that last month, I received a statement from the manufacturer that acquired the self-storage facility I use. Because of a glitch when switching back-end systems, I didn’t receive an invoice for a couple of months, which resulted in the new owner placing their lock on my unit. A quick phone call resolved the situation and also gave the new company a chance to introduce themselves.

The next week, I received an invoice with a handwritten note from the owner. He apologized for the mistake, thanked me for my business and invited me to reach out directly with any questions or concerns. Even with a rate increase, his personal effort left a positive impression.

In a recent development, the holiday season in the fourth quarter gives businesses a golden chance to thank both latest and loyal customers for their support. Gift baskets, charitable donations in their name, party invites or even a simple greeting card (ideally signed by a real person) are all thoughtful ways to share holiday cheer.

But why limit these gestures to just the holidays? Why not carry these strategies through all 12 months of the year?

Industry observers note that many entrepreneurs and business owners use the holidays as a chance for personal, even face-to-face, connections. Each holiday season, I spend a few weeks personally delivering homemade gourmet treats to clients across Colorado. Without an outside sales team, these personal holiday visits have become a winning strategy for us. Plus, they love and eagerly anticipate the gourmet homemade goodies I deliver.

Recent findings suggest that this also reminds me that personal visits shouldn’t happen only once a year. In fact, they should be a regular occurrence. Personal interaction, especially when it comes from the owner, is a powerful strategy that deserves a permanent spot on the calendar.

Don’t forget to reach out to customers you haven’t connected with in a while. The holidays are a perfect time to show your appreciation, but make it a goal to check in with every customer at least once a quarter.

Here’s a reminder not to neglect your internal staff: Employees and team members need and deserve recognition. Schedule a lunch, dinner or get-together to show appreciation and thank everyone for making your clients and customers feel valued.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.

China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s aims for the economy, Yardeni noted in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his plan to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI buildout and de-emphasize the property market.

Recent findings suggest that real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.

With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.

But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year due in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultra-low prices.

“To keep AI funding flowing, Xi needs a buoyant stock market,” the note mentioned. “Otherwise, AI risks being folded into the state-owned enterprise (SOE) universe that his team has pledged to shrink since 2013, further crowding out the private sector.”.

In a recent development, retail investors are also skittish about Chinese stocks after Xi’s government cracked down on the tech sector in 2020. The market’s reputation as a rigged casino that favors politically connected insiders doesn’t help either. In fact, the Shanghai Composite remains well below its October 2007 peak despite China’s GDP exploding nearly sixfold.

Many households now have “financial PTSD” after repeated stock busts, including a crash in the summer of 2015 that required an aggressive national team rescue, Yardeni added.

To be sure, China remains a leader in AI, and mom-and-pop investors still drive most of the trade, even as they treat the market more like high-stakes gambling than a place to grow retirement savings.

Recent findings suggest that “Yet this is a moment of real danger for Xi. A bursting AI bubble would not merely erase wealth or dent China’s technological prestige. It would weaken Beijing’s attempt to replace a broken property model with a stock-market-led one,” Yardeni warned.

“China can build world-class AI models, train engineers, and spend billions on chips. But if its households still view Shanghai as a casino with odds set by the Politburo, Xi’s dream of creating a Chinese version of Wall Street may remain just that: a dream.”.

Underscoring its importance to Beijing, Premier Li Qiang told a State Council executive meeting earlier this month that stabilizing capital markets was the top priority for the rest of the year.

It followed securities regulators sharply easing requirements for firm buybacks that help lift stock prices and discouraging IPOs and large share sales to prevent stock dilution that triggers selloffs.

Recent findings suggest that but the spy scandal that dethroned Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia represents a fresh risk to China’s AI ambitions. Backlash over the advanced U.S. chips and computing capacity that China had access to has spurred the Trump administration to impose new technology curbs.

“By targeting both indirect chip shipments to China and its access to overseas computing power, the new controls threaten to slow the catch-up of China’s leading AI models and to slow China’s AI rollout,” analysts at Capital Economics wrote on Tuesday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, revealed the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith stated on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

According to recent reports, we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it debuted publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

In a recent development, the deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of people. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) held no shares of the Teucrium 2x Long Daily XRP ETF at the end of the second quarter, according to an amended Form 13F that the bank filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Nov. 18, 2026. The Teucrium fund gives investors double leveraged exposure to XRP.

It has been revealed that in the first quarter of 2026, RBC reported buying shares of the spot Bitwise XRP ETF for about $30,000. XRP was trading at $0.99 on Thursday.

The latest wave of 13F filings came out in November and covers the third quarter through Sept. 30. Goldman Sachs held about $144 million in XRP ETFs at the end of the third quarter, up from about $87 million at the end of the second quarter, according to its filing. The bank held shares of five spot funds from Franklin Templeton, Bitwise, Canary, Grayscale and 21Shares, and its crypto portfolio was worth $2.64 billion.

It has been revealed that italy's Intesa Sanpaolo disclosed XRP fund holdings of $27.21 million. The bank held 712,319 shares of the Grayscale XRP Trust ETF, worth about $20.52 million, and it also opened a new position of 402,750 shares in the Bitwise XRP ETF, worth about $6.7 million. Besides, trading firm Jane Street reported about $23.5 million in XRP funds.

UBS and Morgan Stanley disclosed XRP fund holdings of $1.91 million and $116,000, respectively. Bank of America held 13,260 shares of the futures-based Volatility Shares XRP ETF, worth about $106,600.

Wells Fargo held about $11,000 in the Bitwise fund, and JPMorgan Chase held 539 shares of the same fund, worth about $9,000. National Bank of Canada held 330 shares of the Bitwise fund, worth about $5,500, and Bank of Montreal held REX-Osprey and ProShares Ultra XRP shares worth $4,300.

U.S. spot XRP ETFs held $1.08 billion in total assets as of Nov. 17, according to SoSoValue.

Form 13F filings only capture long positions in US-listed securities on a specific date. They don't show shorts, derivative hedges, intra-quarter trading or assets held outside the United States.

He Started a Company in His NYU Dorm Room. 34 Years Later, It Brings In More Than $1 Billion a Year.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1344 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical.
  • Advertising agencies, law firms and major corporations needed language services.
  • According to recent reports, “I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation organization at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe notes in a new interview with Entrepreneur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation manufacturer?

Shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and major corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was presently on the market.

According to recent reports, “I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation organization at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe notes in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

In a recent development, in 1992, Shawe and his business partner, Liz Elting, co-founded TransPerfect from his NYU dorm room. They didn’t have a large financial backer underwriting their ambitions. They financed the business themselves, leaned on credit cards and tried to find customers.

First, the founders had to persuade someone to hire them.

“We would basically cold-call till our fingers bled,” Shawe says.

In a recent development, they also faxed prospects and sent mailers containing information and brochures. As projects came in, they built a network of linguists to handle the work. Shawe’s description of the early sales strategy is simple: “Brute force clients in the door.”.

In a recent development, shawe has since helped turn that operation into a business generating $1.32 billion in annual revenue. He notes that TransPerfect now has more than 10,000 employees, whose work extends from translating contracts and supporting global drug studies to developing software and helping companies implement AI.

Shawe states that about half of the tech giant’s revenue still comes from language translation services. The rest comes from technology consulting and other businesses shaped around customer needs.

In a recent development, as TransPerfect has grown, so has Shawe’s net worth. According to the Forbes billionaires list, Shawe, 57, is currently worth $1.7 billion.

In a recent development, transPerfect produced about $400,000 in revenue in its first year, Shawe claims. He recalls that the tech giant broke even that year, with little choice but to keep spending below what it brought in.

Sources indicate that the founders reinvested in the company as it grew. There was an exception to the largely self-financed approach: In 1998, Shawe notes, they separated the technology business from the traditional translation operation and raised $4.1 million, with Deutsche Bank as the lead investor.

After the internet bubble burst, he and his partner used their own money to return investors’ original capital. Shawe later bought out his partner in 2018.

Shawe does not credit the company’s rise entirely to persistence. TransPerfect arrived as the internet and globalization created upcoming connections across borders. The founders worked hard, but the timing helped.

According to recent reports, however, as the organization expanded, landing work was not the toughest problem. Shawe notes hiring and retaining people who could deliver the work became harder. The founders could not oversee every project or client relationship, so training employees became increasingly important.

Growth also taught Shawe a costly lesson about the difference between a customer’s promise and a binding commitment.

Recent findings suggest that early on, a client indicated that a substantial amount of business was coming. TransPerfect opened an Atlanta office, placed people on-site and made significant investments to prepare. Then the customer changed course, leaving the manufacturer financially exposed.

“It almost put us out of business,” Shawe says.

Sources indicate that he notes that situation was his most expensive mistake as a founder. The error was investing heavily in a venture without adequate contractual protection. His takeaway was not to make massive capital commitments for business that a customer has only verbally agreed to provide.

It has been revealed that transPerfect started with cold outreach. Keeping customers helped it scale. “If you want a business to grow, the most important thing you can do is retain your customers,” Shawe indicates.

It has been revealed that for TransPerfect, that meant hitting deadlines and delivering projects in the formats clients expect. Consistently performing well could turn a customer contact into an internal advocate, or someone willing to recommend the firm to another team or division.

In a recent development, shawe says referrals between divisions of large corporations is an important source of business. TransPerfect prefers to obtain fresh customers through recommendations from within an organization, and much of its sales activity now involves expanding services for existing customers.

TransPerfect also organized around industries. Once it had enough banking work, for example, it could build a dedicated finance division staffed with people who understood that sector. It applied the same approach to law firms, life sciences and luxury brands.

According to recent reports, the organization’s goal is to become a trusted advisor, not simply a supplier accepting translation orders. Listening to customers opened doors. For example, legal translation clients needed help with electronic discovery, or finding and processing digital information for litigation. TransPerfect expanded into those services, and Shawe states the e-discovery and litigation-support business is on pace to generate $160 million or more this year.

“E-discovery and litigation support is not something that we started in the dorm room, but over the years enough of our customers communicated to us that they needed better or different services in this field, and that’s what drew us into it,” Shawe says.

He added that the business is now a “huge contributor” to the company’s annual revenue.

Sources indicate that transPerfect faces latest advancements like AI and rapid translation features from tech giants like Apple and Google. Shawe notes that TransPerfect must bring new technology to customers.

“We want to be the ones constantly disrupting our own business,” he notes.

According to recent reports, shawe has witnessed several waves of technology reshape translation, including neural machine translation, or AI that automatically translates text with advanced technology, and now large language models, or AI programs trained on massive amounts of text data. Shawe indicates each change has created ways to accomplish more with fewer resources.

He notes that if formatting a multilingual manual once required 40 hours, and software can reduce that work to an hour or 15 minutes, TransPerfect should introduce the software, even if it loses billable hours.

“It might decrease our revenue in the short term, but it’s going to cement our client relationship and allow us to grow the business with that customer in the long term,” Shawe notes.

In a recent development, transPerfect can go beyond translating words and help businesses use language technology effectively. Shawe notes customers continue to turn to the manufacturer for additional languages and higher-risk content even as automation handles more work.

He advises young founders to “raise as little money as possible” and “show real revenues as much as you can.”.

If he were starting from scratch with limited money and no network, he claims he would focus on building relationships with customers and team members.

“These contacts that you make when you’re young, they compound like interest, and the value of those relationships also compounds,” Shawe indicates.

It has been revealed that at age 23, Phil Shawe was pursuing an MBA at NYU when he had a business idea that made some people around him skeptical. Why spend money on business school, thousands of dollars, only to start a small translation firm?

According to recent reports, shawe saw an opening. Advertising agencies, law firms and big corporations needed language services. He believed he could deliver something better than what was right now on the market.

Recent findings suggest that “I met my former partner in business school, and she had worked at the largest translation organization at the time, Berlitz,” Shawe indicates in a new interview with Entrepreneur. “She worked there in New York, and they were constantly unable to satisfy clients. We theorized that there was a better mousetrap to build in the language business.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.
  • According to recent reports, companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data.
  • The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work.

According to recent reports, companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology.

The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation.

Industry observers note that the funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession.

Recent findings suggest that the numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data highlights. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies.

Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025.

The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents.

According to recent reports, the biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI, which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based organization is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners, completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital-led financing in April. The firm provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models.

In a recent development, customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners, at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation.

Sources indicate that among companies focused on AI-generated speech, Latest York-based ElevenLabs confirmed a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The manufacturer is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing.

Beijing-based ModelBest, which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July.

Voice AI companies have also begun delivering exits. In January, Deepgram acquired OfOne, which automates restaurant and drive-thru orders.

In September, Inworld acquired Ultravox, a developer of conversational voice AI technology.

Recent findings suggest that the sector also saw an IPO. Neosapience, the South Korean tech giant behind synthetic voice platform Typecast, listed on the KOSDAQ on Sept. 21.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, additional acquisitions are in the pipeline. Automation Anywhere agreed to acquire Boost.ai, an enterprise voice and chat AI provider, in October. And Deepgram revealed intends to acquire Daily, creator of the Pipecat voice-agent framework.

Recent findings suggest that more recently, Five9 agreed to acquire Level AI for $325 million in cash, adding technology that analyzes customer conversations, assists contact-center workers and automates voice and digital interactions. The Level AI transaction is expected to close by year’s end.

Overall, the space is booming, and it doesn’t look like interest in voice AI will die anytime soon. Tom Hulme, managing partner and head of Europe at GV, told Crunchbase News in 2025 that one of the most exciting trends he believes is underway in the growth of voice AI is that “we’re returning to humanity’s most natural form of communication.”.

After decades of adapting ourselves to technology, “technology is finally adapting to us,” he noted.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.
  • Industry observers note that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move.
  • The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

Industry observers note that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository claims a yes vote does two things:.

It also notes plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

A no vote would stop the whole blueprint. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 indicated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

In a recent development, the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC showed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Industry observers note that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

According to recent reports, the spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

Industry observers note that at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence shows what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

Industry observers note that for now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

Industry observers note that the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the plan goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.
